world.era: Bronze-Age Troy and Italy (c. 1180 BC), told from Augustan Rome (29-19 BC)
world.setting: Two worlds, and a shot must never mix them. (1) The poem's world: the burning citadel of Troy, open Mediterranean sea-lanes, the half-built Punic city of Carthage, the misty underworld, and the trench-scarred river plain of Latium — bronze armor, wool and linen, oil lamps, no iron machinery, no stirrups, no domes. (2) The poet's world: lamp-lit Augustan Rome, scroll cases, wax tablets, marble under construction, a fever-bed at Brundisium.
world.register: Documentary-grave and clinical, never heroic-triumphant. The camera watches a man being used up: low light, dust, smoke, salt, exhaustion. When the state's version of events appears (the shield, the parade of souls), it is deliberately gleaming and staged — the contrast IS the argument.
world.imageStyle: ancient Mediterranean antiquity (Bronze-Age Troy c.1180 BC / Augustan Rome 19 BC): bronze armour, horsehair crests, wool tunics and linen, leather sandals, oil lamps, stone and timber; no medieval plate, no modern clothing or objects

aeneas.name: Aeneas
aeneas.role: Trojan prince turned reluctant founder; the subject of the case study. Never drawn exulting — he endures, carries, obeys, and finally breaks.
aeneas.look: Weathered Trojan warrior in his late thirties, dark curling hair and a short beard, dented bronze scale cuirass over a dark red wool tunic, a tawny lion skin across his shoulders, exhausted hollow eyes

anchises.name: Anchises
anchises.role: Aeneas's father; carried out of Troy on his back, later the guide in the underworld who delivers Rome's mission statement.
anchises.look: Frail white-bearded man in his seventies, thin limbs, undyed wool robe, clutching small clay household gods to his chest

creusa.name: Creusa
creusa.role: Aeneas's wife, lost in the smoke of Troy because he did not look back; returns as a ghost who authorizes his departure.
creusa.look: Young Trojan woman with dark hair bound in a linen fillet, pale saffron gown, half-lit in smoke, already spectral

ascanius.name: Ascanius
ascanius.role: Aeneas's young son, the future the mission is for; the small hand in the right hand.
ascanius.look: Boy of about ten, dark curls, short undyed tunic, leather sandals, stretching to keep up with a stride too long for him

dido.name: Dido
dido.role: Queen of Carthage; given the poem's best rhetoric and realest grief, then destroyed by Aeneas's orders from the gods. Her curse summons Hannibal.
dido.look: Regal Phoenician queen in her thirties, black hair coiled with gold, Tyrian purple robe, heavy gold torque, grief held tight in the jaw

turnus.name: Turnus
turnus.role: Champion of the Italians; kills Pallas and wears his sword belt — the object that gets him killed while begging.
turnus.look: Powerful young Italian warrior, bronze helmet with a horsehair crest, bare muscled arms, a wide gold-studded sword belt strapped across his chest

pallas.name: Pallas
pallas.role: Evander's teenage son, entrusted to Aeneas as a ward; his death is the fuse that destroys Aeneas's self-control.
pallas.look: Teenage boy soldier, beardless fine-boned face, light ill-fitting bronze armor, an oversized gold-studded sword belt, far too young for the field

evander.name: Evander
evander.role: Elderly Greek-Italian king on the future site of Rome; hands his only son to Aeneas.
evander.look: Elderly king in a plain undyed wool cloak, silver beard, standing among rough thatched huts on a scrubby hillside

priam.name: Priam
priam.role: Last king of Troy, cut down in his own palace on the night of the fall.
priam.look: Very old king of Troy, white beard, purple-bordered robe over thin shoulders, lit by burning rafters

juno.name: Juno
juno.role: The hostile goddess; ends the war by negotiating the erasure of the Trojan name.
juno.look: Imperious goddess in white and gold drapery, a peacock at her side, cold controlled fury, seated in golden cloud

jupiter.name: Jupiter
jupiter.role: King of the gods; sets the destiny, signs the deal that deletes Troy.
jupiter.look: Bearded king of the gods on a throne of golden cloud, an eagle beside him, storm light behind

venus.name: Venus
venus.role: Aeneas's divine mother; wounded in the Iliad, later commissions the shield.
venus.look: Luminous goddess in pale drapery seen through a haze of light, never fully solid

mercury.name: Mercury
mercury.role: Delivers Jupiter's order to abandon Dido — in broad daylight, so it cannot be dismissed as a dream.
mercury.look: Messenger god with winged sandals and caduceus descending in harsh noon light, short traveling cloak

vulcan.name: Vulcan
vulcan.role: Smith god; forges the shield that shows a future its bearer cannot read.
vulcan.look: Soot-blackened smith god at a volcanic forge, heavy arms, hammer raised, sparks in the dark

augustus.name: Augustus
augustus.role: The patron; the golden climax of the underworld parade and of the shield — and the man who overruled Virgil's will.
augustus.look: Young Roman emperor, clean-shaven, laurel wreath, white toga with a purple border, twin flames at his brow in the shield relief

virgil.name: Virgil
virgil.role: The poet: the other man in the poem being used by the state. Ends feverish at Brundisium asking for the manuscript to be burned.
virgil.look: Roman poet of about fifty, thin drawn face, plain undyed toga, holding a papyrus scroll and a stylus, lamp-lit

lavinia.name: Lavinia
lavinia.role: The Italian princess Aeneas is fated to marry; never consulted, barely speaks.
lavinia.look: Young Italian princess in a saffron veil, eyes lowered, silent at the edge of the frame

cleopatra.name: Cleopatra
cleopatra.role: The enemy on the shield's Actium relief, shaking a sistrum, backed by monstrous Egyptian gods.
cleopatra.look: Egyptian queen on a galley deck, dark linen and heavy gold, shaking a bronze sistrum

hannibal.name: Hannibal
hannibal.role: The avenger Dido's curse conjures — Rome's near-extinction, two centuries later.
hannibal.look: Carthaginian general in a scarlet cloak leading war elephants through a snowbound alpine pass

nisus.name: Nisus
nisus.role: Half of the pair of young Trojan lovers killed on a night raid.
nisus.look: Lean young Trojan soldier, dark stubble, light leather armor, blood-slick hands in the dark

euryalus.name: Euryalus
euryalus.role: The younger of the pair; his death is the poem's most tender writing.
euryalus.look: Beardless boy soldier with fair curls, oversized helmet, light leather armor

lausus.name: Lausus
lausus.role: Young Italian prince killed shielding his tyrant father.
lausus.look: Young Italian prince stepping in front of an older armored man, small round shield raised

troyBurning.look: Narrow Bronze-Age citadel streets at night choked with smoke and corpses, roof beams on fire, bronze glinting in the dark

shore.look: Storm-wrecked Libyan beach at grey dawn, splintered ship timbers, soaked exhausted men, salt haze

carthage.look: A half-built Punic city: scaffolded stone walls, masons at work, Tyrian-purple awnings, cranes against a hot blue sky

underworld.look: Misty grey poplar wood and a slow black river, drifting souls, no sun, ash-coloured light

elysium.look: An expansive misty green plain with its own sun and stars, distant wrestlers and singers, a valley river

olympus.look: A terrace of golden cloud far above a battlefield, two thrones, storm light

latium.look: Trench-scarred Latin river plain, earthworks and ditch-lines, dust, Bronze-Age siege camps

virgilStudy.look: Lamp-lit Augustan Roman room, pigeonholed scroll cases, wax tablets, a single oil lamp, 19 BC

actium.look: The naval battle rendered as relief work on beaten bronze: war galleys, Apollo's drawn bow, a sistrum, barking Anubis

objects.why: The shield of Aeneas: the state's version of history, embossed and gleaming, carried by a man who is 'ignorant of the events'. The book's central image and the video's cold-open callback.
Pallas's gold-studded sword belt. Turnus straps it on as a trophy; the glint of it on his shoulder is what ends the poem. Show it as an object before it is a plot point.
Troy burning, Dido's pyre, Pallas's funeral pyre, and Virgil's own request to burn the manuscript. The same fire runs through every act.
Father on the back, son by the hand, wife lost behind: the load-bearing image of the whole epic and of pietas itself.
The bill: Creusa, Dido, Nisus and Euryalus, Lausus, Pallas, the eight sacrificed youths, Turnus. The casualty report the state did not commission.
The twin gates of sleep — horn for true visions, ivory for false dreams. Aeneas leaves the prophecy of Rome through the ivory one. Needs a real two-door image, not an abstract portal.
'He simulates hope on his features' — pietas drawn as a face held in place over panic. The visual thesis of the episode.
Troy burned, Carthage half-built and abandoned, Rome not yet begun: the city is always either ending or unfinished, never enjoyed.
Dido falls on Aeneas's sword; Aeneas buries his in Turnus's chest on the last line. The same blade closes both women's and men's stories.
The manuscript itself — 11 years of work, ordered burned on the poet's deathbed and published anyway. The frame of the whole episode.
Not glorious conquest: trench warfare, night raids, human sacrifice. Draw it as a slaughterhouse, never as a parade.
'I do not chase Italy of my own free will' — non-consent, the hostage of the gods. Use sparingly and never literally over a real person's wrists.

spine.claim: Rome commissioned a founding myth and got a casualty report: Aeneas arrives as Homer's second-tier survivor, and Virgil turns that weakness into endurance whose cost he then documents.
The mission takes the man apart piece by piece: Creusa lost because he could not look back, Dido destroyed by an order he did not choose, and his own defense is a confession of non-consent.
He goes to the underworld for a meaning he can hold, is handed the empire's mission statement — and Virgil walks him back out through the gate reserved for false dreams.
He carries a history he is not permitted to understand, and when Pallas dies the coping mechanism shatters into human sacrifice and the killing of a suppliant.
The poem stops on that failure, and the poet who asked for it to be burned was overruled by the state — the same machine, working on the man who wrote it.
